title: Explains why horizontal acceleration is zero in equation (1)

asked: Why is the horizontal acceleration zero in equation one? || What would it take to make it non-zero?
answer: looking at the shared notes on projectile motion with the setup and Newton’s law split into horizontal and vertical components. Ready when you want to walk through it. Because we're assuming no horizontal forces — no air resistance, just gravity acting downward. So the horizontal component of Newton’s second law is simply m times x double dot equals zero, which means the horizontal acceleration is zero. You’d need a horizontal force — like air drag, wind, or a push from a rocket. Any nonzero horizontal force makes m times x double dot nonzero, so the horizontal acceleration shows up.
why: It does not state that horizontal velocity remains constant at v0 cos θ throughout the flight.

title: Explains what 'uncoupled' means and when it would break

asked: The notes say the two directions are uncoupled. What does that actually mean here? || Would that still hold with air resistance?
answer: It means the x and y motions don’t affect each other. Gravity only shows up in the y equation, and there’s no x term in it. So you can solve for the horizontal motion without worrying about the vertical, and you handle the vertical separately. They’re independent because there’s no force linking them in this ideal model. Not usually. With air resistance, the drag force depends on the velocity, which has both x and y parts, so the equations get coupled. No. With air resistance, the force depends on the velocity, which has both horizontal and vertical components. That couples the equations, so you can't treat x and y separately in the clean way we do here.
why: It omits total-speed/speed-squared drag and overstates that air resistance always couples the equations; linear componentwise drag can remain uncoupled.
